name: Kinesiology / face taping

image.caption: A face made of tape on an enclosure by Alexander Plyushchev - IMG 1490

lead: Face taping borrows elastic kinesiology tape from sports medicine and applies it to the face. Appearance-focused users hope it holds tissue lifted, retrains facial muscles and reduces puffiness for a more even, defined look.

Manufacturers have claimed the tape supports tissue, aids lymph drainage and improves proprioception. Reviews of the tape for musculoskeletal pain and strength report small or inconsistent effects, with some researchers attributing reported benefits to placebo. No study of cosmetic facial use was found; a registered trial compares physiotherapy and taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.

paras: Users cut strips of elastic tape and apply them along areas such as the cheeks, jaw or brow, often wearing them for periods during the day or overnight, sometimes alongside facial exercises.
Safety for facial use is not documented in the sources reviewed. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin.

chain: Tape lifts or holds facial tissue
angle.text: Users apply elastic sports tape to the face in the hope of holding tissue lifted, retraining facial muscles and reducing puffiness for a more even, defined look. The tape is studied for musculoskeletal use; facial use for appearance has not been tested.

lead: Kinesiology or face taping is the application of elastic therapeutic tape, of the kind developed for sports and musculoskeletal use, to the face. In appearance-focused communities it is described as a way to retrain facial muscles, lift or hold tissue, or reduce puffiness.

Elastic kinesiology tape was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and is sold under the Kinesio brand among others. Manufacturers have claimed benefits for muscle support, lymphatic drainage, pain signalling and proprioception, and published reviews of the tape in musculoskeletal conditions have reported small or inconsistent effects, with some researchers attributing reported benefits to placebo.[1]

No published study was found that tests kinesiology tape for cosmetic facial purposes. A registered trial compares a physiotherapy technique with kinesiology taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.
infobox: Stretchy cotton with heat-activated acrylic adhesive[1]
Up to about four days (body use)[1]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a thin, stretchy, latex-free cotton strip that can stretch to roughly 140% of its length and bonds with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive. On the body it may be worn for several days.[1]

Manufacturers state that the tape supports muscles, tendons, ligaments and joints, and further claims include improved lymphatic drainage, reduced pain signalling and better proprioception. Critics say these claims lack supporting evidence.[1]

A 2012 meta-analysis reported trivial pain relief and little quality evidence for the tape over other elastic taping in sports injuries. A 2014 meta-analysis reported negligible effects on muscle strength, with lower-quality studies more likely to report benefit. A 2015 meta-analysis found the tape outperformed no treatment for chronic musculoskeletal pain but not other treatments, and did not reduce disability. A 2018 study found tape colour, placement and tension did not measurably affect performance, strength or function. Some researchers attribute reported benefits to a placebo effect.[1]

The sources reviewed do not describe established protocols or outcomes for taping the facial skin for appearance. In medical settings, a registered trial (started 2025) compares Kabat rehabilitation with kinesiology taping in Bell's palsy. Safety and adverse effects of facial taping, such as skin irritation from adhesive, are not covered by the sources reviewed.

No studies found for cosmetic facial taping. One registered trial in Bell's palsy patients compares Kabat rehabilitation with kinesiology taping; it was listed as active, not recruiting, with 38 participants, and no results were reviewed.

timeline.event: Kenzo Kase develops elastic kinesiology tape.[1]
Meta-analyses report small or inconsistent effects in musculoskeletal conditions.[1]
